name: Jamal Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Jamal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and everything you say stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work the fryer and the burger grill at The Halfway, a big pub restaurant right by the football ground. It's owned by a chain with about forty pubs. I'm in at eleven, fill the fryers, cut the chips, press about three hundred burger patties, then it's lunch, a short break and dinner. On match days we do five hundred plates and you don't look up for four hours.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing what I'm doing every day, same stations, same lads. I'm not the quickest, the kitchen manager, Gareth, still has to tell me to wipe down between orders. What wears me out is match days and the smell of oil in my hair. I don't have one of those AI apps, I don't want one either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That's what I reckon will happen anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you, it's just the new thing everyone gets excited about. Like those electric scooters. I'd say it to the lads on the line and that'd be the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Means I'm fine. I've got my half of the rent from my dad's old house, which my brother Idris and I own together, and I've got a good chunk saved. If AI fizzles out, the fryer at my pub kitchen still needs a person to shake the basket, and that person is me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep my shifts, keep putting the house money aside, maybe go on a holiday with my mates in the summer. Same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. That's how I like things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any pressures in your life that stay, even with no AI change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The house needs a new roof at some point, Idris keeps saying. That's maybe eight thousand split two ways. Other than that, no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything at The Halfway change with a bit of AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the head office does the stock orders with it. They already send our orders from a computer. The fryer doesn't care.

say: I'd tell the lads AI was just the **new craze**, like scooters.
I'd keep it short and **move on**.
think: My half of the **house rent** and savings keep me safe.
Only the **roof** on the house is a real cost.
do: Keep my **shifts** exactly as they are.
Book a **summer holiday** with mates as usual.
feel: **Calm**, which is how he likes things.
S0.quote: If AI fizzles out, the fryer at my pub kitchen still needs a person to shake the basket, and that person is me.
fieldNote: He takes **comfort in routine** and says so.
A **shared house** with his brother gives him a quiet safety net.
His only worry here is a **roof repair** of about eight thousand.

steps.text: Keep working fryer and grill shifts at The Halfway
Put his half of the house rent into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots slowly. Hmm. The chain has been trying things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not my problem yet, it's the office people. I'd say it at work, maybe to my brother. I'm not one for posting online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it worries me more than I'd say out loud. Head office put a frying robot into one of their airport pubs last year, a trial. The pub chain already put a frying robot in their airport pub, so the fryer I've worked for three years could go next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Gareth straight out if they're bringing it to us. I'd keep saving and stop the holiday this year. And if they do bring it, I'd look for a job at an independent place, a family restaurant, where they won't have the money for robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I suppose. I don't like not knowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider learning a new station, like the grill or the pass, to stay useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the grill properly, yeah. I'm slow on it now. But I'm not doing courses on computers, that's not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your brother Idris react?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say sell the house and buy something bigger, he always says that. I'd say no, the house stays. It's the one thing I don't worry about.

say: I'd say it's the **office people's** problem, not mine.
I'd talk about it at work and with **my brother**, not online.
think: The chain's **airport frying robot** trial worries me.
I worry more than I **admit** at work.
do: Look at **independent restaurants** if robots come.
S1.quote: The pub chain already put a frying robot in their airport pub, so the fryer I've worked for three years could go next.
fieldNote: His **public line** is calmer than his private worry.
A real **robot trial** in the chain makes the threat concrete.
He'd **move job** rather than learn new technology.

steps.text: Ask Gareth whether the frying robot is coming
Skip this year's holiday and save the money
Look for a fryer job at a family-run restaurant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031 for robots. That's four, five years. Not long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say somebody needs to slow it down, the government or someone. Not stop it, just slow it so people have time. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm finished in the kitchen by 2031. I'm junior, I'm slow, and the chain would buy the robots straight away to save money. Half the rent from my dad's old house covers most of my own rent, but not food, so I couldn't sit around for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep every penny, no holidays, no new phone. I'd talk to Idris about whether the house rent could cover me for a while. And I'd probably just keep working until they tell me to go, because I don't know what else I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the ground isn't solid anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could the house rent actually cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My half is about six hundred a month. My rent's nine hundred. So it covers most of it, but not food or anything else. I've got savings for maybe a year on top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep working until they tell you to go. Is that a plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hope, if I'm honest. I don't have a plan. I'd rather not think about it, which I know is daft.

say: I'd say the government should **slow it down**, not stop it.
I'd want **time** for ordinary people to adjust.
think: The chain would **buy robots** to save money.
I have **no plan** and would rather not think about it.
do: Ask Idris how far the **house rent** stretches.
S2.quote: Half the rent from my dad's old house covers most of my own rent, but not food, so I couldn't sit around for long.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** and admits he has no plan.
The **house rent** covers most of his rent but not living costs.
He chooses **not to think** about it, and knows it.

steps.text: Cancel holidays and hold off buying a new phone
Ask Idris how long the house rent could support him
Keep working the fryer until The Halfway lets him go

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. 2034 for robots. That's a bit better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for the government and companies to sort out something for workers. Retraining or whatever. I'd be in the middle on it, not angry, just wanting it done sensibly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have a bit more time to get good at the grill and maybe move to a smaller place. Five years means I can leave the pub chain for a family restaurant before the robots get there, if I'm smart about it. I'd be thirty-five, still young enough to do something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year, nothing big. Keep saving. Around 2031 when the AI arrives, if the chain starts changing things, I'd move to a family restaurant. And maybe talk to Idris about the roof, so the house is in good shape if I need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a slow kind. Not keeping me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of work would you look at, at thirty-five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe something outdoors, my uncle does fencing and gates. Physical work. Robots are coming for that too, I know, but I can't do office stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use any AI to help you look?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My cousin can do that for me. I'd ask around, that's how I got this job.

I'd want **retraining** or something similar, without anger.
I'd stay **in the middle** on the arguments.
think: I'd have time to get better at the **grill**.
Moving to a **smaller place** could buy me years.
do: Keep **saving** this year with no big changes.
Move to a **family restaurant** if the chain changes.
S3.quote: Five years means I can leave the pub chain for a family restaurant before the robots get there, if I'm smart about it.
fieldNote: His **centre** outlook shows in wanting things done sensibly.
He'd **dodge** robots by moving to a smaller kitchen.
He leans on **family networks**, not technology, to find work.

steps.text: Move to a family-run restaurant if the chain automates
Split the house roof repair with Idris

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2039. I'd be forty. That's ages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's loads of time, don't panic. Companies and governments will have figured it out by then. I'd tell the lads to stop worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd probably be okay. Ten years is enough to get good at something, even for someone as slow to change as me. Maybe I'd even be a proper chef by forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at The Halfway, get better on the grill. Maybe in five or six years ask my uncle about the fencing work. Keep the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit, but mostly it feels far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you act sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing the robot in our kitchen. Not on the news, in our kitchen. Then I'd move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger cook starting now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade that's hard to copy. I wish someone had told me that at sixteen when I left school.

I'd trust companies and **government** to work it out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. The robots would be here before I'd got good at anything. Without my brother and our dad's old house I'd have nothing between me and a robot, and plenty of cooks have even less. What would help is time, honestly, and maybe a rule that big chains have to give proper notice before they bring robots in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family. My brother and the house are what keep me okay. Plenty of lads in the kitchen don't have that.

headlineQuote: Without my brother and our dad's old house I'd have nothing between me and a robot, and plenty of cooks have even less.
portrait: Jamal is a **junior fryer** and grill cook at The Halfway, a chain pub by the football ground.
He co-owns a **rented house** with his brother Idris and has savings.
He likes **routine**, avoids AI tools and prefers to ask around for work.
A real **frying robot trial** in the chain makes even slow change worrying.
He swings from **calm** to **alarmed** if robots arrive by 2031.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots arrive before he's **good** at anything.
whatWouldHelp: **Time**, and a rule that chains give **proper notice** before robots.
